catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) There are no phonemic length or tone in Are. Stress in Are is predictable and occurs on the penultimate syllable. If the stressed syllable is a V or CV, stress is realized through lengthening of the vowel in the stressed syllable. ˈbe.sa ‘banana’ ˈku.kou ‘dog’ ni.ˈu.ra ‘coconut’ to.po.to.ˈpo.na ‘name of a fish’ When the penultimate syllable is a CVV, and the word is said in isolation (or as the last word in a string of speech), the only realisation of stress is an exception in the vowel deletion process (see Syllable Patterns below). In this case, the penultimate CVV does not turn into a CV but instead maintains its long character. ˈbau.na ‘different’ si.ˈyau.wa ‘fish, meat’ ˈmai.re ‘shell fish’ ˈdau.wa ‘sleep’ When there is a word final closed syllable, it is likely that the stress goes to the ultimate syllable. In this case no lengthening takes place in the penultimate syllable. However, the ultimate closed syllable does not change in length, pitch or strength either. The same applies to a penultimate closed syllable followed by an open syllable. a.na.ˈkam ‘I will eat.’ ka.bi.ˈtam.ni ‘properly’ [fn. 3, p. 4:] The last consonant in a closed syllable is always the phoneme /m/. From related languages one can see that this /m/ used to be /mu/.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive stress, length or tone. Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is realised mainly as lengthening of the penultimate vowel; a stressed penultimate CVV syllable keeps both vowels (it is exempt from the general CVV->CV vowel-deletion process). Words ending in a closed syllable (the only coda is /m/, historically *mu) probably carry stress on the final syllable instead (a.na.ˈkam), and a closed penult followed by an open final behaves the same way (ka.bi.ˈtam.ni), with no lengthening cue.
new_statements.exceptions: Final closed (/m/-final) syllables likely take the stress (authors hedge: 'it is likely'); penultimate CVV syllables in isolation/pre-pausal position realise stress only by resisting vowel deletion; reduplicated identical vowels merge into one long vowel (apoːˈpopo). Orthographic word division splits inflectional prefixes from the stem, so the phonological word for stress includes prefixes (a.na.ˈkam, to.po.to.ˈpo.na).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the (phonological) word, illustrated with citation forms; CVV behaviour is described relative to pause ('said in isolation or as the last word in a string of speech'). Draft OPD based on 10 months of fieldwork and a 2005 alphabet workshop; villages Mukawa, Bogaboga, Ginada, Irikaba, Wabubu, parts of Dabora.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Are [mwc] = Glottolog aree1239 as spoken at Mukawa, Bogaboga, Ginada, Irikaba, Wabubu and parts of Dabora on Cape Vogel (the 'Are chain' of Are-Taupota); 'Mukawa' (Giblin 1923, Ray 1907) is the older mission name for the same language. No dialect differentiation is made in the stress statement.

The hunt establishes that no later Svensson materials on Are (dictionary, grammar essentials, revised OPD) exist in the SIL archive: Erik Svensson's only other SIL item is the Kakabai [kqf] OPD (49079); the 2015 'Are Lexicon' (93008, Project VITAL) is not by the Svenssons, is a 19-page lexicon, and is not online. new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonemic length or tone; word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable, realised as vowel lengthening in an open (V/CV) penult and as retention of the full CVV (no vowel deletion) in a CVV penult; a word ending in a closed syllable probably carries stress on that final syllable (a.na.ˈkam, ka.bi.ˈtam.ni), with no lengthening anywhere.
new_statements.exceptions: word-final closed syllable: stress 'is likely' to go to the ultima (hedged); penultimate closed syllable followed by an open syllable: no lengthening; CVV penult keeps its long character only in isolation / phrase-finally.
new_statements.identity_note: Are [mwc] (older name Mukawa), Are chain of Are-Taupota, Nuclear Papuan Tip; OPD title page: Cape Vogel, Milne Bay Province; major villages Mukawa, Bogaboga, Ginada, Irikaba, Wabubu and parts of Dabora; data from 10 months of fieldwork and an Alphabet Development Workshop, Oct 17-21 2005 (BTA / Wycliffe Sweden).
